content.title: About
content.content: Carrots, frozen, cooked, fat added is a ready‑to‑eat product made from fresh carrots that have been blanched, quickly frozen, and then cooked with added vegetable fat. The product retains most of its nutrients, a characteristic sweet flavor, and a tender texture, making it convenient for fast meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Freezing preserves over 90 % of the carrot’s vitamin A and beta‑carotene.
Cooking with added fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
Frozen vegetables are widely used in the food‑service industry for ready‑made soups and stews.
Carrots are one of the most popular vegetables worldwide and are part of the staple diet in more than 150 countries.
Rapid freezing maintains cell structure, so carrots stay slightly crisp even after cooking.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Enhanced vitamin absorption thanks to fat
items.content: The added vegetable fat improves the bioavailability of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Relatively low in calories
items.content: Even with added fat, the product remains modest in calories, suitable for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the oil used in the product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Industrial processing may include added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Vitamin loss over long storage
items.content: Extended frozen storage can lead to a slight decrease in vitamin C levels.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: The soft texture can pose a choking risk for toddlers; serve under supervision.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to use: add it to soups, stews, pasta, rice or potato dishes, or simply heat it in a pan with a little oil. For extra flavor, sprinkle fresh herbs, spices, or incorporate it into salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen carrots in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

egg-whole-baked-no-added-fat.title: Egg, whole, baked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: A baked whole egg with no added fat is a simple way to prepare a nutrient‑dense food that retains most of the vitamins and minerals found in a raw egg. The egg is baked in the oven at a moderate temperature, resulting in a tender yet fully cooked product.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable sources of complete protein.
Baking without added fat preserves the egg’s natural flavor and aroma.
Eggs are rich in choline, which is important for brain health.
Baked eggs are often used as a base for salads, sandwiches, and quick meals.
Vitamin D content in eggs increases slightly with heat treatment.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: One egg provides about 6 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamins B2, B5, and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of choline
items.content: Choline is vital for liver function and cognitive processes.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption and supports bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Eggs contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may develop an allergic reaction to egg proteins, which can be severe.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: A large egg contains about 186 mg of cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor intake.

items.title: Risk of salmonella
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor Salmonella bacteria; baking until fully set reduces this risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked eggs can be eaten on their own as a snack, diced into salads, added to sandwiches, or used as a topping for vegetable dishes. They keep well in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store baked eggs in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Discard if they develop an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled mushrooms are fresh or boiled mushrooms that have been preserved in a brine made with vinegar, salt, sugar, and aromatic spices. They have a distinctive tangy‑sour flavor, a firm texture, and a long shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled mushrooms are a staple in Eastern European, Russian, and Middle Eastern cuisines.
Traditional brine includes vinegar, salt, sugar, bay leaf, mustard seeds, and black pepper.
Mushrooms absorb the spice aromas, and their flavor deepens over time – they are best after 2‑3 days.
In Russia, pickled button mushrooms are often served as a snack with vodka.
Pickled mushrooms are sold in glass jars as well as vacuum‑sealed pouches.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms provide niacin, riboflavin, and biotin, which support metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup of pickled mushrooms contains about 30 kcal, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Selenium and polyphenols in mushrooms help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Beta‑glucans found in mushrooms stimulate the body’s immune response.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled mushrooms often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Presence of preservatives
items.content: Commercial products may contain preservatives that can cause sensitivity in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: If mushrooms are not properly cooked before pickling, there is a risk of botulism.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled mushrooms are enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, pastas, pizzas, or used in hot dishes such as stews and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: After opening, keep in the refrigerator in a sealed jar for up to 2‑3 weeks. Avoid using a utensil that has touched other foods to prevent contamination.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-seafo.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce, Seafood and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: This is a home recipe for whole‑grain pasta tossed in a smooth cream sauce with seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid) and added vegetables (broccoli, carrot, bell pepper). The dish is rich in fiber, protein and healthy fats, making it a balanced and nutritious meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta contains more fiber and micronutrients than regular white pasta.
The cream sauce, made with cream and Parmesan, gives a velvety texture without heavy butter.
Seafood such as shrimp and mussels are excellent sources of omega‑3 fatty acids.
Quick sautéing of broccoli and carrot retains most of their vitamins.
A homemade recipe lets you control salt levels and add favorite herbs like garlic, basil, or a pinch of paprika.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Seafood combined with whole grain provides a complete amino acid profile.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Shrimp and mussels help maintain cardiovascular health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Broccoli, carrot and bell pepper supply vitamins C, K, A and potassium.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta raises blood sugar more slowly than white pasta.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels or squid.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cream sauce and added salt can increase sodium intake; adjust seasoning accordingly.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Use lactose‑free cream or a plant‑based alternative if needed.

items.title: Potential contaminants
items.content: Seafood may contain trace heavy metals; choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Cook whole‑grain pasta until al dente. In a pan, sauté garlic, add seafood and cook 2‑3 minutes. Add vegetables and stir‑fry briefly. Pour in cream, add grated Parmesan, and simmer until thickened. Toss with the pasta, season with salt, pepper and fresh herbs. Serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. The cream sauce may separate; gently reheat and stir before serving. Do not freeze the dish with seafood, as texture may deteriorate.

content.title: About
content.content: Air‑popped popcorn with added butter is a light, crunchy snack. The popcorn is first popped without oil, then a small amount of melted butter is mixed in to give a rich, buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Air‑popped popcorn contains less fat than traditional oil‑popped popcorn.
Butter is added after popping to preserve the crisp texture of the kernels.
Popcorn is one of the most popular cinema snacks worldwide.
The corn used for popcorn is the only variety that ‘pops’ when heated.
Popcorn can be used in salads, desserts, and even as a coating for fried foods.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Air‑popped popcorn without added oil provides about 30 kcal per gram, making it a good option for weight control.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Popcorn is a source of dietary fiber, which supports digestive health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Corn kernels contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Popcorn is naturally gluten‑free, suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Popcorn provides B1, B3 and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If salted butter is used, the sodium level can be high, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Butter may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to milk proteins.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: The light texture can lead to rapid consumption of large portions.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Using partially hydrogenated butter can introduce trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to movie‑night mixes, tossed into salads, or sprinkled with spices or cheese. For a richer taste, gently reheat the popcorn with a little extra butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated to prevent the butter from going rancid.
